I wish writers would stop using the "Why doing [vague action] results in [desirable result]. For all you know, their entire argumentation could be complete utter bullshit.

That's a good point. Journalism should strive for accurately representing clear facts and let the reader create an informed conclusion. Editorials have their time and place, but I don't like how reporting and editorializing have been mixing more and more.

It's a light version of clickbait, really. It's identical to the headline "Did [notable politician or other figure of public life] spend Thanksgiving with an Indonesian child prostitute?" that you might find on the front of a newspapers, only to buy the rag and find a minimal article on it's last page which details that said public figure had actually spent Thanksgiving with its family, and that the entire rest was unconfirmed rumors.

I think it's because writers see it as a "value add". That dozens of other sites might be reporting this story, but we're the only ones who can give our unique take on the news. It makes it difficult for anyone looking for coverage for niche subverses like /v/CoOpGaming, /v/IndieGames, or /v/RetroGaming.

Though I find that theory reasonable, I would argue that there would be much more "additional value" if they really left out the why. A headline is supposed to both draw attention and give a short overview of the article. The entire "why the Imps in Doom actually are innocent victims" nonsense may help with the further but fails at the latter - the "why" question is purely a means to draw in further readers when your actual argumentation is to weak or completely trivial.
